candidateRows: A beginningless temporal series cannot exist because it would instantiate an actually infinite collection, whose concrete existence is metaphysically impossible.
This is Craig's principal actual-infinity argument for the finitude of the past and directly supports the Kalam premise under discussion.
Craig distinguishes actual from potential infinity, states a three-step argument against a beginningless past, and uses Hilbert's Hotel to motivate its crucial metaphysical premise.
The strange consequences of infinite collections do not establish metaphysical impossibility unless an actual contradiction or stronger reason for impossibility is supplied.
The move attacks the key inference from Hilbert-style counterintuitive consequences to the impossibility of any concretely instantiated actual infinity.
Craig's claim that Hilbert's Hotel demonstrates the metaphysical impossibility of a concrete actual infinity.

Malpass explains the structural property behind Hilbert-style examples, questions whether their consequences contain contradictions, and argues that apparent strangeness is not an infallible guide to impossibility.
On a tensed theory of time, an infinite past would already contain an actual infinity, whereas an endless future remains finite at every stage and grows only potentially.
This supplies a temporal asymmetry intended to defeat the Aristotelian classification of a beginningless past as merely potentially infinite.
Malpass's account of Aristotle's view that both an infinite past and an infinite future can be potentially rather than actually infinite.

Craig argues that succession proceeds toward later times, so mentally counting backward must not be confused with temporal formation; a beginningless past would have completed infinitely many elapsed events at every moment.
Hilbert-style scenarios need not contain logical contradictions to reveal metaphysical impossibility, and quantum mechanics does not furnish an adequate counterexample to that inference.
The move directly defends the actual-infinity argument's crucial modal inference against Malpass's demand for contradiction and his appeal to empirically accepted strangeness.
Malpass's contention that counterintuitive absurdity is insufficient for impossibility and that quantum phenomena illustrate why strangeness can be real.

Craig concedes that the scenarios are not formally contradictory, offers another infinite-object illustration, distinguishes interpretations of quantum mechanics, and confines Cantorian infinity to the conceptual realm.
The quantum comparison can be conceded as limited while Benardete-style paradoxes still fail to settle the issue because their author defended the possibility of actual infinity.
The correction undercuts Craig's reliance on an authority and family of examples offered to strengthen the inference from bizarre consequences to metaphysical impossibility.
Craig's rejection of the quantum analogy and his appeal to Benardete-style examples as cumulative support against real actual infinities.

Malpass grants that quantum mechanics is only a loose analogy, then notes that Benardete developed striking paradoxes while remaining willing to accept actual infinity rather than treating them as decisive refutations.
Craig's rejection of a beginningless past can be mirrored against an endless future, creating an internal consistency problem for anyone who regards such a future as possible.
This is Malpass's principal symmetry objection to the actual-infinity case, challenging whether its rationale can support a finite past without also excluding an endless future.
Craig's argument that a beginningless past is impossible because it would contain an actually infinite number of temporal events.
Malpass characterizes the challenge as a nonfallacious ad hominem consistency test, mirrors past praises with future praises, and asks Craig to identify a defensible temporal symmetry breaker.
The mirrored-future objection exposes no defect in the argument for a finite past and functions only as an indirect challenge to people holding specified further beliefs.
Craig's first answer attempts to insulate the actual-infinity argument from the future symmetry challenge by denying that the challenge identifies any fallacy in its reasoning.
Malpass's claim that the actual-infinity reasoning applies with equal force to an endless future and therefore pressures Craig's other commitments.
Craig distinguishes a direct objection from an internal-consistency challenge and says the latter targets only those who also affirm immortality, angels, God, or comparable future commitments.
The symmetry objection applies to anyone who accepts the mere possibility of an endless future, not only to theists or people committed to actual immortal beings.
The clarification broadens the objection beyond special theological doctrines, preventing Craig from limiting its relevance to a narrow class of antecedently committed believers.
Craig's characterization of the symmetry argument as targeting only people with commitments such as immortality, angels, or God.
Malpass explains that no actual endless afterlife or immortal subject need be affirmed; accepting that an endless future is metaphysically possible is enough for the mirrored challenge.
If the objector merely assumes that an endless future is possible, the symmetry challenge is question-begging; otherwise it remains an indirect ad hominem objection.
This response addresses the broadened modal version of the symmetry objection and argues that it still neither refutes nor identifies a flaw in the finite-past argument.
Malpass's clarification that the mirrored argument requires only belief in the possibility, rather than actuality, of an endless future.
Craig argues that asserting the possibility of an endless future without defeating his argument assumes the disputed conclusion, while treating the challenge as internal remains merely indirect.
The symmetry objection commits its proponent to the radical impossibility of every world whose temporal series begins but never ends, thereby imposing a substantial burden of proof.
The move challenges the modal cost of Malpass's symmetry principle by arguing that it rules out even potentially infinite futures in all possible worlds.
Malpass's proposed temporal mirroring between the impossibility of a beginningless past and the impossibility of an endless future.
Craig derives from the proposed symmetry that no possible temporal history may have a beginning without an end, labels that consequence radical, and assigns its defender a heavy justificatory burden.
Without an adequate symmetry breaker, the relevant possibilities should treat past and future temporal extent symmetrically.
This directly develops the central objection that arguments excluding a beginningless past may also threaten an endless future unless a principled asymmetry is supplied.
Craig's claim that denying a beginningless past while accepting an endless future imposes a radical metaphysical burden.
After Craig characterizes temporal symmetry as a radical commitment, Malpass says he is uncertain about finitude itself but argues that asymmetric temporal possibilities require a symmetry breaker.
A tensed theory of time supplies the needed past-future asymmetry because future events do not yet exist and remain only potentially infinite.
The proposed asymmetry is essential to preserving the Kalam finitude argument while allowing an endless future, directly addressing a principal challenge to the motion.
Malpass's contention that past and future must be treated symmetrically unless a genuine metaphysical symmetry breaker is identified.
Craig distinguishes an endless but always finite potential future from a beginningless past, grounding the distinction in objective temporal becoming on a tensed theory of time.
Past events can constitute an instantiated infinity even though they no longer exist, whereas future events have never been instantiated.
This supplies the ontological distinction on which Craig's past-future asymmetry depends and explains why present nonexistence does not place past and future events on equal footing.
The objection that presentism makes past events no more real than future events and therefore cannot support the proposed asymmetry.
Craig says past events have existed and entered reality through their causes, while future events have not, then contrasts tensed and tenseless theories and their consequences.
Presentism does not break temporal symmetry because past events do not exist now while future events will exist, and Craig shifts improperly into the future-perfect tense.
This attacks the main metaphysical device used to reconcile a finite past with an endless future and therefore bears directly on whether the philosophical support is adequate.
Craig's contention that objective temporal becoming distinguishes instantiated past events from unreal future events and defeats temporal symmetry.
Malpass argues that correctly tensed claims restore symmetry, illustrates his point with marbles accumulated in a jar, and says Craig changes from simple future to future-perfect claims.
An actually infinite collection cannot be formed by successive addition, while the temporal series of past events has been formed in precisely that way.
This is the principal successive-addition argument named in the motion, supported by the planetary-orbit example and the Grim Reaper contradiction.

Craig presents the formal successive-addition argument, contrasts temporal formation with simultaneously given sets, and illustrates the alleged absurdity through planetary revolutions and Grim Reapers.
Infinite collections require different cardinality concepts, and the inability to reach an infinite ordinal does not show that endless counting lacks aleph-null cardinality.
This challenges the inference from the impossibility of reaching a first infinite ordinal to the impossibility of an endless process having countably infinite cardinality.
Craig's successive-addition argument and its claim that planetary revolutions and counting expose the impossibility of forming an actual infinite.
Malpass treats the planetary example as familiar infinite-set behavior, concedes that no infinite number is reached by counting, but distinguishes ordinal reachability from cardinality.
From the fact that an endless counter can count every natural number, it does not follow that the counter will count all natural numbers.
The every-versus-all distinction is Craig's direct logical answer to Malpass's cardinality objection and supports the claimed impossibility of completing an infinite sequence.
Malpass's argument that an endless counting process reaches each natural number and therefore has aleph-null cardinality despite reaching no infinite ordinal.
Craig distinguishes being able to count every number from counting all numbers and parallels this with traversing the distance from each past event without traversing the entire past.
The every-to-all inference is not invalid in every instance, and Craig has not shown why it fails for an endless counter who encounters each natural number.
This contests whether merely identifying a quantifier pattern defeats the specific endless-counting case, keeping the core challenge to the successive-addition argument intact.
Craig's claim that moving from counting every natural number to counting all natural numbers commits a scope or composition fallacy.
Malpass compares invalid and truth-preserving instances of similar inference patterns, then returns to an ideal endless counter and asks why that particular inference is false.
Successive addition cannot convert a potential infinite into an actual infinite, as the Tristram Shandy story shows despite every page eventually being written.
The response restates the foundational successive-addition principle and gives a focused illustration of why satisfying every finite task does not amount to completing the whole infinite task.
Malpass's demand for a case-specific reason why an endless counter's counting every natural number does not entail counting all natural numbers.
Craig says actual infinities in set theory are given tenselessly rather than generated, then argues that Tristram Shandy leaves no page unwritten without ever completing the autobiography.
Craig conflates simple-future claims with future-perfect claims: always having counted only finitely many numbers does not preclude eventually counting every number.

This targets the tense and quantifier reasoning underlying Craig's potential-infinite response and offers a direct explanation of how every number may be counted without a completed finite-stage total.
Craig's Tristram Shandy argument that completing each individual finite task never constitutes completion of the entire infinite sequence.

Malpass explains future-perfect tense through a completed drinking example and argues that finite future-perfect totals do not settle the distinct simple-future proposition about counting all numbers.
An endless future never contains an actually infinite number of completed events, even if there is no later standpoint from which the whole process is surveyed.
This preserves Craig's asymmetry between an endless potential future and a completed actual infinite, which is central to answering the future-parity objection.
Malpass's claim that Craig illicitly moves from simple-future claims to future-perfect claims about completing an infinite count.

Malpass had argued that an infinite future can contain all counting events without there ever being a future time at which the count has been completed; Craig denies that an actual infinite ever results.

Craig's reverse-countdown discussion appears to contain a distinct impossibility argument: at every earlier time the counter supposedly should already have finished, leaving no time at which counting occurs.
The reverse-countdown scenario is a direct formulation of the successive-addition case against a beginningless past, and Malpass isolates the inference on which its alleged impossibility depends.
Craig's reverse-countdown argument that a person counting from infinity should already have finished at every earlier point.

After setting aside their dispute about future counting, Malpass turns to the past-directed analogue and distinguishes an explanatory objection from an argument that the countdown could never be underway.

If having infinitely much time and a one-to-one correspondence suffices to finish a reverse countdown, the counter should have finished at every earlier time, contradicting the hypothesis that he counted eternally.
This is Craig's direct defense of a successive-addition argument against a beginningless sequence, culminating in an internal contradiction for the proposed eternal countdown.
Malpass's suggestion that Craig's explanatory and already-finished considerations are separate arguments whose relationship is unclear.
Craig explains that the countdown puzzle, the sufficient-condition response, the regress to earlier completion times, and a modest explanatory principle are successive stages of one dialectic.
Infinitely many prior counting events are necessary for finishing a reverse countdown now but are not sufficient, so they do not imply that the counter should have finished earlier.
The objection targets the key modal inference in Craig's reverse-countdown reasoning and, if successful, blocks the claimed contradiction without denying an infinite past.
Craig's inference from the counter's having infinitely much prior time to the conclusion that he should already have completed the countdown.
Malpass accepts that finishing now entails infinitely many prior counts but argues that the converse fails because an eternal counter could presently have any finite number still remaining.

An infinite amount of time paired one-to-one with the numbers leaves nothing further needed for completion, unless one denies any explanatory requirement for why completion occurs at one time rather than another.
This directly supplies Craig's defense of the disputed sufficiency premise and connects the reverse-countdown contradiction to a modest principle of sufficient reason.
Malpass's claim that infinitely many elapsed counting events make present completion possible but do not make earlier completion necessary.
Craig responds that infinite time plus the stipulated correspondence appears sufficient for finishing and says the remaining escape requires rejecting an explanation for the selected completion time.
A modest partial explanation can account for finishing now—such as having ten numbers left ten minutes ago and counting one per minute—even if it does not explain the entire infinite history.
The move challenges Craig's explanatory fallback by offering the kind of non-entailing, mystery-displacing explanation that a modest principle of sufficient reason appears to require.
Craig's contention that an eternal countdown offers no adequate explanation for finishing today instead of at an earlier time.
Malpass distinguishes partial explanation from an entailment-producing total explanation, illustrates the distinction with a causal chain, and then gives a local rate-based explanation of completion.
The relevant modest principle of sufficient reason is defensible yet still violated by a countdown that finishes at one point rather than another, because no adequate explanation selects that point.
This maintains the explanatory component of Craig's reverse-countdown case after Malpass offers a local partial explanation and identifies the precise alleged defect in the scenario.
Malpass's proposed partial explanation that the counter finishes now because ten numbers remained ten minutes earlier at a fixed counting rate.
Craig does not reconstruct the published principle from memory, but insists that its modest formulation is plausible and that an eternal countdown cannot explain its particular completion point.
Grim Reaper arguments do not presently provide a settled objection because their beginning-of-time reasoning may be temporally mirrored to imply that the future must also have an end.
The proposed temporal mirror bears directly on whether an infinity-based paradox supports a beginning asymmetrically or instead generates an unacceptable parallel conclusion about the future.
The audience question invoking Pruss's Grim Reaper and Hilbert's Hotel argument against a backwards-infinite sequence of events.
Malpass cannot identify a premise-by-number response on the spot, refers to related work on accumulation, and emphasizes a possible future-directed mirror of the Grim Reaper reasoning.
Causal finitism breaks the alleged past-future parallel because no event may have infinitely many causes, excluding a beginningless causal past without excluding an endless forward causal series.
The argument offers an alternative philosophical route to a finite past that directly answers Malpass's symmetry objection while allowing the future to remain endless.
Malpass's suggestion that Grim Reaper-style arguments for a temporal beginning can be mirrored to establish an end of the future.
Craig recommends Pruss's causal-finitist treatment as a way to avoid temporal parallelism by imposing finitude on the causal ancestry of an event rather than on every temporal series.
Malpass's position is skeptical rather than beginningless-past advocacy: dismantling arguments that the universe began does not establish that the universe had no beginning.
This clarifies the con side's exact burden on the motion: the critique contests whether the infinity arguments adequately support a beginning, not whether a beginning is false.
Malpass says his most plausible objections disarm positive beginning arguments; he offers no positive case for an infinite past and regards familiar arguments against a beginning as implausible.
A beginningless sequence does not entail the possibility of Hilbert's Hotel when only finitely many rooms can be created at any one time.
This directly contests a proposed route from a backward-infinite sequence to Hilbert's Hotel and therefore challenges support for the past's finitude.
Pruss's claim that a backward-infinite sequence would make Hilbert's Hotel possible.
After the moderator presents Pruss's Hilbert's Hotel and Grim Reaper argument, Malpass rejects its first premise by imposing a finite creation constraint.
Several reformulations of the actual-infinity argument avoid Malpass's symmetry objection concerning past and future infinities.
The move argues that Malpass's principal symmetry criticism does not defeat alternative formulations supporting the impossibility of an infinite past.
Malpass's symmetry-based critique of arguments against an actually infinite past.
Following Malpass's response to the Pruss formulation, Craig stresses that work by Hedrick, Loke, and Pruss supplies formulations outside the symmetry objection's reach.
Counting indefinitely passes every finite natural number but never completes all natural numbers or arrives at actual infinity.
The distinction is essential to Craig's successive-addition case because it denies that endless finite counting ever constitutes a completed infinite total.
The suggestion that counting past every natural number amounts to counting infinitely many items.
A viewer asks whether indefinite counting counts infinitely many objects because every natural number is eventually passed; Craig answers with the potential-infinite distinction.
The relevant claim is that every natural number will be counted, not that counting reaches a final stage at which infinity is completed.
This reframes the successive-addition dispute around quantification over each member rather than completion, preserving Malpass's challenge to Craig's inference.
Craig's claim that indefinite counting never arrives at infinity or completes all natural numbers.
Malpass responds that Craig is again substituting the absence of a completed terminal moment for the distinct question whether each number will be counted.
From the fact that every member of an infinite series is finitely removed from an endpoint, one cannot infer that the whole series is finite.
The alleged every-to-all inference is presented as the core logical error in Malpass's treatment of endless counting and a beginningless temporal series.
Malpass's claim that counting each natural number is sufficient for counting infinitely many numbers.
Craig answers Malpass by comparing future counting with an infinite past, where each event can be finitely distant from the present without the total being finite.
Craig has not established that Malpass commits an every-to-all fallacy, and a fully drawn countermodel is needed to resolve the dispute.
The move rejects Craig's diagnosis of the central logical mistake and identifies the missing demonstration needed before the successive-addition objection succeeds.
Craig's accusation that Malpass repeatedly makes an illicit inference from every member to all members.
Malpass characterizes the exchange as an impasse, says Craig's comments have not shown an actual fallacy, and requests a concrete countermodel before conceding the point.
The Grim Reaper argument is the theistic argument Malpass finds hardest to resolve, although he does not yet regard that as making it decisive.
This concession identifies the strongest unresolved pressure on Malpass's infinity critique and qualifies the certainty of his opposition to beginning arguments.
Asked which arguments he finds most compelling, Malpass distinguishes persuasiveness from unresolved difficulty and singles out the Grim Reaper paradox as hardest to put to rest.
A tenseless theory of time is compatible with a universe having an earlier spacetime boundary and a potentially infinite future expansion.
The move clarifies that a cosmological beginning need not depend solely on a tensed theory and connects boundary evidence to a finite past and endless future.
In response to a question about compatibility, Craig says tenseless time permits an earlier spacetime boundary while current expansion evidence permits an unending potential future.
The Kalam's causal premise and beginning premise jointly support a timeless, spaceless, immaterial, powerful, and personal cause of the universe.
Craig's closing synthesis states the affirmative case, combining the debated philosophical arguments with astrophysical evidence and drawing the intended theistic conclusion.
Craig closes by defending both Kalam premises, citing philosophical and astrophysical support for a finite past, and deriving the attributes of a personal creator.
The central dispute remains unresolved because Craig and Malpass disagree over the inference between each member and the whole, while the required tensed theory is itself controversial.
Malpass's closing synthesis challenges both the logical core of the successive-addition defense and the controversial temporal framework required for Craig's Kalam case.
Craig's defense of the every-to-all distinction and his claim that tensed time is crucial to the Kalam.
Malpass closes by emphasizing disagreement over quantification, controversy surrounding tensed time, an apparent communicative impasse, and his lack of an adequate received rebuttal.
